In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular basis of exercise-induced mitochondrial remoulding and redox-regulation of stress responses.
the molecular mechanisms of age-related decline and the molecular adaptations to exercise training that might offset this decline.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the elderly have a diminished exercise-induced redox response, at least for some of the redox-sensitive stress proteins measured to date, but that mitochondrial responses are preserved.
exercise improves mitochondrial and red ox regulated stress responses in the ageing muscle and that the response is better late than never.
exercise-induced mitochondrial and redox responses are not impaired with age in human skeletal muscle and, therefore, the adaptive responses to exercise training in the ageing muscle are intact.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
exercise-induced mitochondrial remoulding and redox stress responses are not impaired in older skeletal muscle.

exercise-induced mitochondrial and redox stress responses are preserved or even enhanced in elderly human skeletal muscle, and this is likely to underpin the beneficial effects of lifelong exercise training on age-associated declines.
exercise training in the ageing human is a powerful stimulus that improves mitochondrial function and the redox stress response.
The main takeaway from our work is that
exercise training is a potent intervention to improve mitochondrial and redox stress responses in the ageing population.
it is never ‘too late’ for exercise training to promote mitochondrial remodelling and redox homeo-stasis and that these adaptations may offset age-related physiological declines.
exercise training in the older population is not only safe and beneficial but also that the response to training is comparable to that observed in the younger population.
